web_evidence.title: Noble House by James Clavell (Ebook)
web_evidence.note: The licensed Blackstone Publishing preview supplies a sustained prologue and the start of Chapter One. Both externally narrate Dunross and other characters in third person, including their actions and private perceptions, without a participating narrator.

web_evidence.title: James Clavell Writing Styles in Noble House: A Novel of Contemporary Hong Kong
web_evidence.note: The study guide explicitly identifies the book's point of view as third person and distinguishes the narrator's scene-setting from the characters' extensive dialogue.

web_evidence.title: The Protagonist Problem
web_evidence.note: The narrative-structure essay includes Noble House among tapestry novels written in 'multiple third,' with point of view shifting among characters rather than to a participating narrator.

search_log: Searched "Noble House" "James Clavell" excerpt, first chapter, and Google Books; opened the Everand/Blackstone preview, which exposes the prologue and Chapter One in sustained third person.
Searched "Noble House" third person, point of view, narrator, and multiple third; opened the explicit BookRags whole-book description and the Uncanny Magazine structural essay.
Searched "Noble House" epistolary, diary, first person, and multiple narrators; found no credible evidence of sustained first- or second-person base sections.
Opened Hachette's publisher page, but its excerpt control did not expose prose to the web reader; used it only for discovery, not person evidence.
Opened Google Books and Open Library edition records; they verified the 1981 Delacorte work but offered only catalog or snippet material, so they were not used as person evidence.
person_note: The controlling voice is nonparticipating third person, using a multiple-third or omniscient structure that moves among many characters. Goodreads q02517 and q02526 independently expose third-person scene or focal narration, while nearly all visible I, we, and you forms occur in dialogue, thought, aphorism, or paratext. The licensed opening preview agrees, and two explicit whole-book sources describe third-person narration. No researched source supports sustained narration in another person; the main limitation is that the Tier A prose source covers only the opening, offset by interior quote evidence and whole-book structural descriptions.
